- **medium** `missing` penal / referí — (not in the list) → Add `penal = penalty kick` and `referí = referee` (futbol, L1). Ex: "¡Fue penal! El referí no vio nada." _(Basic match talk, different from Spain's penalti/árbitro.)_
- **medium** `missing` empanada / milanesa — (not in the list) → Add `empanada = filled pastry` and `milanesa = breaded steak` (comida, L1). Ex: "Pedimos una docena de empanadas." _(The two most eaten dishes are absent (only the slang `milanga` is there).)_
- **medium** `missing` choclo — (not in the list) → Add `choclo = corn` (comida, L1). Ex: "Una empanada de choclo, por favor." _(Seen on every menu; neutral Spanish maíz is not used for food.)_
- **medium** `missing` cortado — (not in the list) → Add `cortado = espresso with a little milk` (comida, L1), plus `lágrima` and `café con leche`. Ex: "Un cortado y dos medialunas." _(The default café order in Buenos Aires.)_
- **medium** `missing` panza — (not in the list) → Add `panza = belly` (cuerpo, L1). Ex: "Me duele la panza." = My stomach hurts. _(The normal word; cuerpo has pupo and cogote but not panza.)_
- **medium** `missing` pollera — (not in the list) → Add `pollera = skirt` (casa/ropa, L1). Ex: "Me compré una pollera nueva." _(The list has `pollera tubo` (pencil skirt) but not the base word.)_
- **medium** `missing` auto / manejar — (not in the list) → Add `auto = car` and `manejar = to drive` (ciudad, L1). Ex: "¿Sabés manejar?" = Can you drive? _(Ciudad has many car parts (paragolpes, luz de giro) but not the two basic words.)_
- **medium** `missing` cumple — (not in the list) → Add `cumple = birthday (party)` (noche or charla, L1). Ex: "El sábado es el cumple de Sofi." _(Said instead of cumpleaños nearly always; the list has rare `cumplemés` instead.)_
- **medium** `missing` charlar — (not in the list) → Add `charlar = to chat, talk` (verbos, L1). Ex: "Nos quedamos charlando hasta tarde." _(The theme is called 'charla' but the verb is not taught.)_
- **medium** `missing` putear — (not in the list) → Add `putear = to swear at, insult` (puteadas, L1). Ex: "El colectivero me puteó." = The bus driver swore at me. _(The theme is called puteadas and the base verb is missing.)_
- **medium** `missing` caer — (not in the list) → Add `caer = to show up` (verbos, L1). Ex: "Caé a casa tipo nueve." = Come over around nine. _(Used in every invitation; meaning is not 'to fall'.)_
- **medium** `missing` andar (no anda) — (not in the list) → Add `andar = to work, to run (machines)` (verbos, L1). Ex: "El wifi no anda." = The wifi isn't working. _(Daily use; the list teaches the slang `funcar` but not the normal word.)_
- **medium** `missing` colgar — (not in the list) → Add `colgar = to forget; to stand someone up` (verbos, L1). Ex: "Perdón, colgué, ¿era hoy?" = Sorry, I forgot, was it today? _(Very common; only the adjective colgado is there.)_
- **medium** `missing` clavar el visto — (not in the list) → Add `clavar el visto = to read a message and not answer` (expresiones, L1, WhatsApp). Ex: "Le escribí y me clavó el visto." _(Core WhatsApp/dating phrase; add also `mandar un audio` = send a voice message.)_
- **medium** `missing` histérico / histeriquear — (not in the list) → Add `histeriquear = to flirt and then pull away` (noche, L2). Ex: "Me histeriquea hace meses." = He's been playing games with me for months. _(Key Buenos Aires dating word with no simple translation.)_
- **medium** `missing` medio — (not in the list) → Add `medio = kind of, a bit` (charla, L1). Ex: "Estoy medio cansado." = I'm kind of tired. _(Softener used in almost every conversation.)_
- **medium** `experience` vulgar words outside puteadas — paja, pedorro (charla L1); al pedo, ni en pedo (expresiones L1); empedarse, chupar, falopa, merca, frula, transa (noche); pendejo (gente); yuta (ciudad, 'Rude slang'); calentarse ('also horny') → Decide one rule. Either move pedo/paja/drug words into puteadas, or keep them out and also move the mild ones (boludo, gil, otario, cornudo) out. Now en pedo / a los pedos are adult but al pedo / ni en pedo are not. _(The adults-only line is not consistent, so some users see crude words and others miss mild ones.)_
- **medium** `experience` puteadas: otario, mamerto, cornudo, bagayo, turro, franelear, kuka, villero — otario = fool [puteadas, L2, vulgar] etc. → Move otario and mamerto to lunfardo/gente, kuka to politica (next to gorila, zurdo, facho, planero), turro to gente; keep only real swear/sex words in puteadas. _(These are not vulgar; kuka is a political jab like the ones already in politica.)_
- **medium** `experience` lunfardo L1 — lunfardo level 1 = 4 cards (cabrero, chirola, quilombo, trucho); 37 of 49 cards are level 3 → Move quilombo and trucho to charla L1 (everyday words). Make lunfardo an optional 'tango-era' theme, or fill L1 with living lunfardo (laburo, guita, mina, morfar, gil, chamuyo, fiaca, atorrante). _(Less than one pack at level 1; the two L1 words are not 'classic tango-era' to a learner.)_
- **medium** `experience` vesre L1 — vesre level 1 = 3 cards (garpar, ortiba, telo); theme total 18 → Move feca and jermu to L1 and add sope, bolonqui, choborra, or merge vesre into lunfardo as one 'word games & old slang' theme. _(First vesre pack cannot be filled with level-1 words.)_
- **medium** `experience` casa theme — casa = 84 cards (50 at L1), about half are clothes (buzo, campera, remera, bombacha, corpiño, malla, ojotas...) plus hair/office items → Split into `casa` (home) and `ropa` (clothes). Move aro, bordó, abrochadora, birome, valija out of 'home'. _(Biggest theme, and its name does not match half of its content.)_
- **medium** `experience` theme balance — comida 79, casa 84, charla 77 vs vesre 18, campo 34 (15 at L3), animo 34, cuerpo 35; comida L1 = 55 cards, many are produce (alcaucil, zapallo anco, cebolla de verdeo, castaña de cajú) → Cut produce/tool/gaucho items; grow charla, animo, plata and noche with the missing everyday words. _(Volume goes to supermarket nouns and gaucho history, not to what people say in conversation.)_
- **medium** `repetitive` same-meaning cards — 'tell on someone' x6: buchón, botón, buchonear, botonear, mandar al frente, quemar · 'skip school' x3: ratearse, hacerse la rata, hacerse la chupina · 'exhausted' x4: detonado, hecho pelota, quemado, fusilado · 'very busy' x4: a full, a mil, estar hasta las manos, hasta las pelotas · 'head' x3: marote, sabiola, zabeca · 'crazy' x4 → Keep the 1-2 most used of each set (buchón/buchonear, ratearse, hecho pelota, a full + hasta las manos) and say what is different on the others. _(Same English line on many cards; quizzes cannot tell them apart and it feels like filler.)_
- **medium** `experience` golazo — golazo = great news [charla, L1, Celebration] → golazo = great goal [futbol, L1, Also: great success] _(Main meaning is a great goal; the other use only makes sense from football.)_
- **medium** `experience` guarda / conductor — guarda = conductor [ciudad, L3] · conductor = TV host [gente, L2] → guarda = train ticket inspector _(English 'conductor' is unclear, and another card says conductor means TV host.)_
- **medium** `experience` bajón — bajón = shame, sad thing [animo, L1] → bajón = a pity, something sad (qué bajón = what a pity) _('shame' reads as embarrassment for non-native English readers.)_
- **medium** `experience` darle — darle = want to sleep with [puteadas, L1, vulgar] → Card: `le doy = I would sleep with him/her`; or drop. (darle also = to go ahead: 'dale', 'dale que va') _(As a bare word darle mostly means 'go for it'; the sexual use is one fixed phrase.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` juguera — juguera = blender [casa, L2] → juguera = juicer (blender is licuadora) _(A juguera makes juice from fruit; a blender is a licuadora.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` aguante — aguante = let's go! [futbol, L1, Cheer of support] → aguante = support, loyalty; '¡Aguante Boca!' = Go Boca! _(It is a noun (support, endurance) and needs a name after it; 'let's go' is vamos.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` sobre el pucho — sobre el pucho = without planning [expresiones, L2] → sobre el pucho = right away, on the spot _(Means immediately; the list's own `ipso pucho = right away` is the same idea.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong?` mufa — mufa = bad luck [animo, L1] → mufa = bad mood; also: person who brings bad luck _(In the moods theme the meaning is bad mood (tener mufa); bad luck is yeta.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` orto — orto = sheer luck [puteadas, L1, vulgar, Crude] → orto = ass; also: pure luck (de orto) _(Main meaning is ass; cerrar el orto and romperse el orto are in the same theme.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` careta — careta = too proper, doesn't party [gente, L1, Mild teasing] → careta = fake, two-faced; also: sober, doesn't party _(The most common sense today is fake/hypocrite.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong?` mandarse — mandarse = to make a mistake [verbos, L1] → mandarse = to go and do something boldly (mandarse una macana = to make a big mistake) _(Alone it means to go ahead and do it; the mistake is in what follows.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong?` conchudo — conchudo = lazy jerk [puteadas, L2, vulgar] → conchudo = nasty, mean person _(In Argentina it means a mean, bad person, not lazy; and it repeats pajero's line.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong?` gato — gato = weak person [puteadas, L1, vulgar] → gato = nobody, servant-type loser (insult); also: escort _('Weak' misses both real uses.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong?` pito — pito = marijuana cigarette [noche, L2] → Remove (use porro). If kept: pito = willy (child word); whistle _(Rare for a joint; everyone understands pito as penis.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` merequetengue — merequetengue = mess, chaos [charla, L2] → Remove. _(Not Argentine (Mexican/Caribbean word); porteños say quilombo, lío, despelote.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` llavear — llavear = to lock [verbos, L3] → Remove. _(Not used in Buenos Aires (northern provinces/Paraguay); porteños say 'cerrar con llave'.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` arrorró — arrorró = lullaby [charla, L2] → Remove. _(A baby song word in the everyday-talk theme; no use for an adult learner.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` grupo — grupo = a lie, nonsense [charla, L1, Not 'group'] → Move to L3 as old slang, or remove. _(Rare today; learners will only meet grupo = group (e.g. WhatsApp group).)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` cesto de basura — cesto de basura = trash can [ciudad, L2] → Replace with `tacho (de basura) = trash can`. _(Formal sign wording, not Argentine speech; people say tacho.)_
- **medium** `level` mal — mal = a lot, really [charla, L2, Intensifier] → Move to L1. _(Used all day by under-40s ('me gusta mal', '—¿Tenés hambre? —Mal').)_
- **low** `missing` fútbol 5 — (not in the list) → Add `fútbol 5 = five-a-side football` (futbol, L1). Ex: "Los martes juego fútbol 5 con los pibes." _(What people actually play each week; more used than fulbito/picado.)_
- **low** `missing` sándwich de miga — (not in the list) → Add `sándwich de miga = thin crustless sandwich` (comida, L1). Ex: "Compré sándwiches de miga para el cumple." _(At every birthday and office party; unique to Argentina.)_
- **low** `missing` asado cuts: tira de asado, mollejas, chinchulines, matambre — (not in the list) → Add at least `tira de asado = short ribs` and `mollejas = grilled sweetbreads` (comida, L2). Ex: "¿Pedimos mollejas de entrada?" _(Parrilla menus use them; list has vacío, entraña, achuras but not the most ordered ones.)_
- **low** `missing` cubierto — (not in the list) → Add `cubierto = table charge at a restaurant` (comida, L2). Ex: "¿Cobran cubierto?" = Do you charge for the table? _(Appears on bills and surprises foreigners.)_
- **low** `missing` cola — (not in the list) → Add `cola = butt (polite)` (cuerpo, L1) with note: also 'line/queue'. Ex: "Me caí de cola." _(Everyday neutral word; only the vulgar culo/orto are in the list.)_
- **low** `missing` medias — (not in the list) → Add `medias = socks` (casa/ropa, L1). Ex: "No encuentro las medias." _(Basic clothing word that differs from calcetines.)_
- **low** `missing` anteojos — (not in the list) → Add `anteojos = glasses` (casa or cuerpo, L1). Ex: "¿Viste mis anteojos?" _(Everyday word that differs from gafas.)_
- **low** `missing` frazada — (not in the list) → Add `frazada = blanket` (casa, L1). Ex: "Pasame una frazada, hace frío." _(Everyday home word that differs from manta; rarer `acolchado` is in.)_
- **low** `missing` parada — (not in the list) → Add `parada = bus stop` (ciudad, L1). Ex: "¿Dónde está la parada del 60?" _(Needed with bondi/colectivo/SUBE, which are all cards.)_
- **low** `missing` encarar — (not in the list) → Add `encarar = to go up and talk to someone you like` (noche, L1). Ex: "Dale, andá y encarala." _(The list has the adjective `encarador` but not the common verb.)_
- **low** `missing` una bocha — (not in the list) → Add `una bocha = a lot` (charla, L1). Ex: "Había una bocha de gente." _(As common as `una banda`; easily confused with the card `bocho`.)_
- **low** `missing` nomás — (not in the list) → Add `nomás = just, only` (charla, L2). Ex: "Pasá nomás." = Go ahead, come in. / "Acá nomás." = Right here. _(Typical Argentine particle with no direct translation.)_
- **low** `missing` qué macana — (not in the list) → Add `macana = a pity; a mistake` (charla, L2). Ex: "¡Qué macana! Se me rompió el celu." _(The list has the old `macanear` but not the still-used noun.)_
- **low** `missing` tarado / pavo — (not in the list) → Add `tarado = idiot` (stronger) and `pavo = silly` (soft) (gente, L1). Ex: "No seas pavo, vení." _(Everyday mild insults that are not vulgar; pavada is in but not pavo.)_
- **low** `missing` atar con alambre — (not in the list) → Add `atado con alambre = fixed badly, just holding together` (expresiones, L2). Ex: "Este país está atado con alambre." _(Iconic Argentine expression, used about work, cars, the economy.)_
- **low** `missing` remarla — (not in the list) → Add `remarla = to keep struggling on` (expresiones, L2). Ex: "Con esta inflación hay que remarla." _(Very current money/work expression.)_
- **low** `missing` ponerle onda — (not in the list) → Add `ponerle onda = to make an effort, be positive` (expresiones, L1). Ex: "Dale, ponele onda." = Come on, make an effort. _(Six onda cards exist but not this very common one.)_
- **low** `missing` bajar un cambio — (not in the list) → Add `bajar un cambio = to calm down, slow down` (expresiones, L1). Ex: "Bajá un cambio, no es para tanto." _(Common in any argument or stressful moment.)_
- **low** `missing` verdes — (not in the list) → Add `verdes = US dollars` (plata, L2). Ex: "Lo vendió en diez mil verdes." Also note `gamba = 100 pesos` on the gamba card. _(Money talk constantly switches to dollars; dólar blue, cueva, arbolito are cards.)_
- **low** `missing` vesre still in use: sope, bolonqui, choborra, dorima — (not in the list) → Add `sope = pesos`, `bolonqui = mess`, `choborra = drunk`, `dorima = husband` (vesre, L2). Ex: "¿Cuántos sope sale?" _(Vesre has only 18 cards and 3 at level 1; these are more used than dolape/zabeca.)_
- **low** `missing` punga — (not in the list) → Add `punga = pickpocket` (lunfardo or ciudad, L2). Ex: "Cuidado con los pungas en el subte." _(Useful safety word in the city; classic lunfardo that is still alive.)_
- **low** `missing?` nashe / literal / cringe — (not in the list) → Add a small 2020s youth pack: `nashe = great`, `literal = exactly, really`, `cringe`, `re god`. Ex: "Quedó nashe." _(List has ahre and ghostear but little else from current teen/TikTok talk; these may age fast.)_
- **low** `experience` campo theme — bagual, baguala, chiripá, matrero, tropilla, yerra, tapera, rebenque, boleadoras, facón, pulpería... → Keep about 12 (gaucho, estancia, chacra, tranquera, yuyo, tambo, peón, paisano, payada, chamamé, zamba, jineteada) and add peña, chacarera, alpargatas, poncho. Mark the rest as optional 'gaucho history'. _(A learner in Buenos Aires will not hear half of these; they read like a museum list.)_
- **low** `experience` lunfardo L3 — 37 tango-era words: bulín + cotorro, minusa + percanta + papusa, piantar + espiantar + piantado, funyi, gayola, morlaco, fané... → Keep about 15 a learner meets in tango lyrics (percanta, bulín, malevo, compadrito, bacán, gotán, cafishio, mishiadura, piantado, otario); drop near-duplicates. _(Many cards have the same meaning and none is heard in today's speech.)_
- **low** `repetitive` police words — cana = cops (gente) · gorra = police, cops (ciudad L1) · yuta = police, cops (ciudad L1) · rati = cop (vesre) → Put them in one theme, keep cana at L1, move gorra/yuta/rati to L2 with a register note (hostile). _(Four cards, three themes, same English; yuta and gorra are hostile words, not level-1 vocabulary.)_
- **low** `repetitive` word families — kirchnerismo + kirchnerista + cristinista + camporista + kuka · peronismo + peronista + justicialista · chamuyo + chamuyero + chamuyar · escabio + escabiado + escabiar · hincha + hinchada + hinchar · mufa + mufar + yeta → One card per family with the other forms inside the card (e.g. peronismo/peronista). Free the slots for missing words. _(About 15 cards teach a form the learner could guess.)_
- **low** `experience` corner-shop cards — almacén = corner store · chino = corner supermarket · kiosco = corner kiosk · polirubro = corner shop · kiosquero = corner-shop owner → almacén = small grocery store · chino = small supermarket (Chinese-run) · kiosco = candy and cigarette shop · drop polirubro. _(Four 'corner' lines look the same; the learner cannot tell which shop sells what.)_
- **low** `experience` English line format — agarrar = take, grab · chequear = check · gorrear = cheat on · calentarse = get mad · embolarse = get bored · acomodarse = get an easy job · ir a los bifes = get to the point · darle = want to sleep with → Start every verb line with 'to' (to take, to check, to get mad...), as the other 150 verb cards do. _(Inconsistent verb format; without 'to', 'check' or 'cheat on' can be read as nouns.)_
- **low** `experience` flag text — luca [1,000 pesos] · arrorró = lullaby [Lullaby] · vigilante [Pastry] · dar manija [Encourage] · caño/enganche/morfón/taponazo [Football] inside the futbol theme · tener las pelotas llenas [vulgar, Vulgar] · [Crude] on only 4 of 70 puteadas → Remove flags that repeat the English line or the theme; use one fixed set (Old-fashioned, Regional, Careful, Filler, Not 'x'). _(Many flags carry no information and the labels are not consistent.)_
- **low** `experience` Old-fashioned cards at level 2 — guarangada, merequetengue, deschavetado, mersa, mino, pijotero, estar pato, copetín, piluso, soutien, lungo, macanear, al divino botón, dar un pesto, hacerse el sota → Move every card flagged Old-fashioned to L3 (or to one 'what grandma says' pack). _(Words the app itself calls old-fashioned come before current ones.)_
- **low** `experience` level order in file — bolche [politica, L3] sits between L2 cards; culear [puteadas, L3] sits between L2 cards → Move both lines after the L2 block so file order = level order. _(Packs are dealt in file order, so these level-3 cards land in a level-2 pack.)_
- **low** `experience` aguaviva — aguaviva = jellyfish [ciudad, L1] → Move to L2 in a beach/nature pack with bañero, parador, malla, ojotas. _(A jellyfish is not a city word and not level 1.)_
- **low** `experience` colimba — colimba = military service [politica, L2] → Move to lunfardo/old words L3 with note 'ended in 1994'. _(Not politics, and military service has not existed for 30 years.)_
- **low** `experience` toco — toco = a lot [plata, L2] → toco = a pile (of money) [plata, L2] ('un toco de guita') _(Without context it reads like a general 'a lot' and repeats una banda/chorrera.)_
- **low** `experience` fierro / fierros — fierro = gun [ciudad, L2] · fierros = weights [cuerpo, L2] · chumbo = gun [lunfardo, L2] → One card: fierro = piece of iron; slang: gun; fierros = gym weights. Drop chumbo or mark it old. _(Two cards for one word in different themes, and two gun cards.)_
- **low** `experience` cero — cero = zero [charla, L1, Before a noun] → cero = no ... at all (cero ganas = no desire at all) _('zero' teaches nothing; the Argentine use is the meaning.)_
- **low** `experience` alto — alto = a huge [charla, L1, Before a noun] → alto = great, really good (alto asado = a great barbecue) _('a huge' is not a full meaning and misses the 'great' sense.)_
- **low** `experience` tildado — tildado = frozen [animo, L2] → tildado = stuck, not reacting (person or computer) _('frozen' alone reads as cold.)_
- **low** `experience` PH — PH = house behind a house [casa, L2, Real estate] → PH = low apartment with its own street entrance, no building fees _(Current line is not what a PH is in a rental ad.)_
- **low** `experience` flaco / loco — flaco = man, guy [Not 'skinny'] · loco = man, buddy [Not 'crazy'] → Flag: "Also: skinny" / "Also: crazy" _(Both words also keep their normal meaning; 'Not' is misleading.)_
- **low** `experience` pararse — pararse = to stand up [verbos, L1, Not 'to stop'] → Flag: "parar still means to stop: pará = wait" _(Learner will hear 'pará!' (stop/wait) all day; the flag suggests the opposite.)_
- **low** `experience?` pete — pete = loser [puteadas, L2, vulgar, Gamer slang] → pete = blowjob; insult: loser _(First meaning is sexual; the learner should know why it is vulgar.)_
- **low** `experience` partido — partido = county, district [ciudad, L2] → partido = district of Buenos Aires province (Also: match; political party) _(The common meanings (match, party) are missing, so the card confuses.)_
- **low** `experience?` spelling variants — ortiba · ballottage · sanguche → ortiva (most common spelling) · balotaje · sánguche _(Learners will see the other spelling in chats and news.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` apurar — apurar = to pressure [verbos, L2, "Also: hurry"] → apurar(se) = to hurry [L1, Also: to pressure someone] _(Main, everyday meaning is to hurry (apurate!).)_
- **low** `en_wrong?` caraculo — caraculo = idiot [puteadas, L2, vulgar] → caraculo = sour-faced, always-angry person _(Comes from 'cara de culo' = angry face, not stupidity.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` napo — napo = Neapolitan pizza [comida, L2] → napo = pizza (or milanesa) with tomato slices and garlic _(Argentine napolitana is a topping, not Naples-style pizza.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` tener pinta — tener pinta = to look good [expresiones, L1] → tener pinta de = to look like, to seem (tiene buena pinta = it looks good) _(Without 'buena' it means 'to look like'.)_
- **low** `en_wrong?` quedar pagando — quedar pagando = to look silly [expresiones, L2] → quedar pagando = to be left waiting / left with no answer _(Idea is being left hanging, not looking silly.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` bancar — bancar = to put up with [verbos, L1, "Also: back someone"] → bancar = to support, back someone; to wait (bancá = hold on); to put up with _('Te banco' and 'bancá' are the uses a learner hears most.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` micro — micro = coach, bus [ciudad, L1] → micro = long-distance bus _('coach' is unclear for B1 readers and it is not the city bus (that is colectivo/bondi).)_
- **low** `en_hard` patovica — patovica = security guard [noche, L1] → patovica = nightclub door guard _(A patovica is only the big guard at a club door.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` funebrero — funebrero = funeral worker [gente, L3] → Remove. _(Too rare to be useful.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` cumplemés — cumplemés = month anniversary [gente, L2] → Remove; add `cumple` instead. _(Niche teen word.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` hombre de la bolsa — hombre de la bolsa = scary man who takes kids [gente, L2] → Remove or move to a culture card. _(A children's bogeyman, not vocabulary a learner needs.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` batero — batero = drummer [gente, L1] → Move to L3 or remove. _(Niche musician word sitting at level 1.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` topadora — topadora = bulldozer [ciudad, L2] → Remove. _(Very rare in daily life.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` desgrabar — desgrabar = to transcribe [verbos, L2] → Remove. _(Journalist jargon.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` tool and garden items — bordeadora, cortadora de pasto, mecha, flor de la ducha, pata de rana, alfiler de gancho, gomera, payana, lampazo, cama marinera, semipiso, pollera tubo → Remove most; keep at most 2-3. _(Hardware-store nouns; nobody needs these to talk like a local.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` car parts — paragolpes, luz de giro, cubierta, guinche → Keep goma, baúl, patente, registro, nafta; drop these four. _(Mechanic vocabulary; cubierta repeats goma (tire).)_
- **low** `not_relevant` sortija — sortija = merry-go-round ring [ciudad, L2] → Fold into the calesita card. _(Two cards for one children's ride.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` soutien — soutien = bra [casa, L2, Old-fashioned] → Remove (corpiño is the card). _(Old duplicate of corpiño.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` acomodarse — acomodarse = get an easy job [plata, L2] → Fold into `acomodado`. _(Same idea as the L1 card.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` desaprobar / chequear / cansador — desaprobar = to fail · chequear = check · cansador = tiring → Remove or mark as 'normal Latin American Spanish'. _(Not slang and not specially Argentine; desaprobar also repeats bochar.)_
- **low** `not_relevant?` chorrera — chorrera = a lot [charla, L2] → Remove (una banda, un montón, una bocha cover it). _(Uncommon, and another 'a lot' card.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` alfonsinista / menemismo / cristinista — alfonsinista = Alfonsín supporter [L3] · menemismo [L2] · cristinista [L1] → Remove; one card `-ista / -ismo` explains the pattern. _(History-book words built by a rule.)_
- **low** `not_relevant?` PASO — PASO = primary elections [politica, L2] → Add flag 'suspended since 2025' or remove. _(The open primaries were suspended, so the word is leaving daily use.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` frula / mamúa / troncho / festichola — frula = cocaine · mamúa = being very drunk · troncho = marijuana cigarette · festichola = party → Remove or keep in one 'old slang' pack. _(Dated duplicates of merca, en pedo, porro, joda.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` bichito de luz / bicho bolita / mamboretá / zorrino — bichito de luz = firefly [campo, L1] ... → Move to L3 'nature' or remove. _(Small animals are not a priority and sit at level 1 of campo.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` chanchito — chanchito = piggy bank [plata, L1] → Move to L2/L3. _(Child's object among core money words.)_
- **low** `level` morfi — morfi = food [comida, L2] → Move to L1 (morfar is already L1). _(Very common, and its verb is level 1.)_
- **low** `level` entraña — entraña = skirt steak [comida, L2] → Move to L1. _(One of the most ordered cuts at any parrilla.)_
- **low** `level` pulóver — pulóver = sweater [casa, L2] → Move to L1. _(Basic clothing word; chomba and riñonera are L1.)_
- **low** `level` manguear — manguear = to ask for money [verbos, L2] → Move to L1. _(Very common verb (cigarettes, money, favors).)_
- **low** `level` barra brava — barra brava = violent football fans [futbol, L2] → Move to L1. _(In the news every week; more useful than botinera or figurita.)_
- **low** `level` microcentro / el interior / country — microcentro, el interior, country [ciudad, L2] → Move to L1. _(Core geography words; aguaviva, bañero, banquina are L1 instead.)_
- **low** `level` ranchar — ranchar = to hang out [verbos, L3] → Move to L2. _(Current youth word, not rare.)_
- **low** `level` escabiar — escabiar = to drink alcohol [noche, L3] → Move to L2 with escabio / escabiado. _(The verb is as common as its noun, which is L2.)_
- **low** `level?` quebrar — quebrar = to get very drunk [noche, L3] → Move to L2; line: 'to throw up or pass out from drinking'. _(Common among young people.)_
- **low** `level` bailanta — bailanta = cumbia dance hall [noche, L1] → Move to L2. _(Dated word; less useful than after, escabio, gira which are L2.)_
- **low** `level` falopa / transa — falopa = drugs · transa = drug dealer [noche, L1] → Move to L2. _(Drug dealing is not first-pack going-out vocabulary.)_
- **low** `level` botinera — botinera = footballer's girlfriend [futbol, L1] → Move to L2. _(Gossip-TV word, not core football.)_
- **low** `level` corralito / cristinista — corralito = frozen bank accounts [politica, L1, 2001 crisis] → Move to L2; bring cepo, gremio, ñoqui up to L1. _(History term at L1 while current terms sit at L2.)_
- **low** `level` cabrero / chirola — cabrero = angry [lunfardo, L1] · chirola = very little money [lunfardo, L1] → Move to L2. _(Both sound dated; not first-pack words.)_
- **low** `level` comida L1 produce — alcaucil, castaña de cajú, cebolla de verdeo, zapallo anco, cubanito, chocolatín, pan lactal, tapa [comida, L1] → Move to L2. _(Shopping-list nouns ahead of fainá, entraña, morfi.)_
- **low** `level` casa L1 objects — abrochadora, telgopor, bolsa de dormir, cucha, riñonera, mamadera [casa, L1] → Move to L2. _(Rarely needed objects at level 1 of the biggest theme.)_
- **low** `level` epa / calorón / flor de / chimento — epa, calorón, flor de, chimento [charla, L1] → Move to L2. _(Less frequent than L2 cards like mal, de diez, sonaste.)_
- **low** `level?` estar en la lona / de onda / mandar al frente — [expresiones, L2] → Move to L1. _(More common than L1 cards like pisar el palito or si te digo te miento.)_

### slang1

- **high** `tip_unclear` paja — vulgar: false · note: "Me da paja": I can't be bothered... Also slang for masturbation. → Set vulgar: true (or add to note: 'Crude. Only with friends, never at work or with older people. Polite option: "me da fiaca".'). _(It is a coarse word; a learner saying 'me da paja' to a boss or in-laws will embarrass themselves.)_
- **medium** `not_argentine` improlijo — es: improlijo → Replace the card word with 'desprolijo' (example: 'El trabajo está bien, pero es muy desprolijo.'). Note: opposite of 'prolijo'. _(Argentines say 'desprolijo'; 'improlijo' is rare and sounds bookish.)_
- **medium** `not_argentine` rugbier — En esa fiesta había puros rugbiers de colegio privado. → Esa fiesta estaba llena de rugbiers de colegio privado. _('Puros' meaning 'only' is Mexican/Chilean; a porteño says 'estaba lleno de' or 'eran todos'.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` afanador — es: afanador · en: thief → Remove the card, or replace it with 'afanar' (to steal / to rip off): 'Me afanaron el celu en el subte.' _(Almost nobody says 'afanador'; people say 'chorro'. The useful word is the verb 'afanar'.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant?` chorrera — "Una chorrera de" means loads of something. → Remove the card. Argentines say 'una banda de', 'un montón de', 'una pila de', 'un toco de'. _('Una chorrera de' is Caribbean/Venezuelan usage; rarely heard in Buenos Aires.)_
- **medium** `not_argentine?` de más — Enthusiastic agreement among young people: "—¿Vamos? —¡De más!" → Remove the card, or tag it 'Uruguay'. The Argentine answer is '¡De una!' (already a card). _('De más' as 'great / sure' is Uruguayan; in Buenos Aires it is not the normal reply.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant?` merequetengue — A fun word for a chaotic mess or fuss. Playful, used by all ages. (tag: Old-fashioned) → Remove the card (quilombo, bardo, lío cover it). If kept: level 3 and delete 'used by all ages'. _(Rare and dated in Argentina; the note contradicts its own 'Old-fashioned' tag.)_
- **medium** `level` grupo — level: 1 · "Es un grupo" means it's made up. A "grupero" is someone who makes stuff up. → Move to level 3 with tag 'Old-fashioned'. Note: '"Es grupo" means it's made up. Old lunfardo, mostly older people.' Drop 'grupero'. _(Dated lunfardo, not a level-1 word. Usual form is 'es grupo' with no article; 'grupero' is hardly used.)_
- **medium** `not_relevant` arrorró — es: arrorró · en: lullaby · theme: charla → Remove from the slang pack (or move to a culture/kids pack). _(Not slang and not specifically Argentine; a learner will never say it in conversation.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` pendejo — In Argentina it means a kid or teenager, often dismissive. Rude in Mexico, careful. → Add: 'Coarse in Argentina too: never use it for someone's child in front of them. Also means an immature person. Feminine: pendeja.' Consider vulgar: true. _(The note makes it sound safe in Argentina; it is disrespectful and fairly crude here as well.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` careta — en: too proper, doesn't party → en: 'fake, two-faced'. Note: 'Someone fake or hypocritical who keeps up appearances. Also someone who doesn't drink or do drugs.' Example: 'Es un careta, te sonríe y después habla mal de vos.' _(Main meaning today is fake/hypocrite; the no-party sense is secondary.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` mino — en: handsome guy · tag: Old-fashioned · example en: Did you see the new handsome guy at the gym? → en: 'guy'. Note: 'Masculine of "mina": a guy, often an attractive one. Said mostly by women.' Example en: 'Did you see the new guy at the gym?' Remove the Old-fashioned tag. _(It just means a guy; it is still current, not old-fashioned; the English example is awkward.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` potro — en: very attractive person · note: An attractive person, literally a colt. → en: 'very handsome man'. Note: add 'For a woman: "potra".' _('Potro' is only for men; a learner would call a woman 'un potro'.)_
- **medium** `weird?` olvidate — —¿Me ayudás con la mudanza? —¡Olvidate! Ahí estoy. → —¿Está buena la serie? —Olvidate, es lo mejor que vi este año. (en: 'Is the show good? —Absolutely, it's the best thing I saw this year.') _(After a request for help, '¡Olvidate!' reads as 'forget it'. The 'absolutely' sense appears when confirming an opinion.)_
- **medium** `missing` mal — Youth slang intensifier after a verb: "me gusta mal"... → Add to note: 'Alone, "¡Mal!" means "totally, so true": —Qué frío hace. —Mal.' _(The stand-alone agreement 'Mal' is the most common use and would confuse a learner who hears it.)_
- **medium** `tip_wrong` minga — Casual, a bit cheeky but not a swear word. (no tag, level 2) → Add tag 'Old-fashioned', level 3. Note: 'A cheeky "no way!". Mostly older people now; a bit rude, so only with people you know.' _(Dated word, and rougher than the note says (it comes from an Italian vulgar word).)_
- **medium** `experience` boludez / pavada, buchón / botón, de una / de más, cheto / concheto, grasa / mersa, bárbaro / joya — Pairs share the same or almost the same 'en' line (e.g. boludez = pavada = 'silly thing'; buchón = botón = 'someone who tells on others'). → Make each main line different, e.g. boludez: 'silly thing (a bit rude)'; pavada: 'silly thing (polite)'; botón: 'informer, rat (older word)'. _(In a quiz the learner cannot know which word is asked for, and the register difference is lost.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` plato — "¡Qué plato!" means how hilarious. (no Old-fashioned tag) → Add tag 'Old-fashioned' and move to level 3. _(Mostly said by older people; young porteños do not use it.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` papa frita — tag: Playful insult · level 2 → Add 'Old-fashioned' to the tag/note and move to level 3. _(A dated, childish insult; rarely heard from adults today.)_
- **low** `not_relevant?` banana — "Hacerse el banana": to act cocky or smart. → Add 'A bit old-fashioned' to the note; the current word is 'hacerse el canchero'. _(Slang from the 80s-90s; understood, but sounds dated.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` funebrero — es: funebrero · en: funeral worker → Remove the card, or keep only at level 3 and add 'Also the nickname of Chacarita football fans.' _(Niche job word, not useful for conversation in a slang pack.)_
- **low** `level` batero — level: 1 → Move to level 2 or 3. _(Niche music word sitting next to core words like 'pibe' and 'chabón'.)_
- **low** `level` tincho — level: 1 → Move to level 2 (same as 'rugbier'). _(A social stereotype joke, not basic everyday vocabulary.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear` boleta — "Sos boleta": you're in big trouble, as a joking threat. → Note: '"Sos boleta": literally "you're a dead man". Among friends and family it is a joke: you're in big trouble. As a normal noun...' _(The literal meaning is a death threat; the learner should know it is only safe as a joke.)_
- **low** `missing` capo — Someone great at something or just a great person. "Sos un capo" is high praise... → Add: 'For a woman: "sos una capa".' Same for 'groso' → 'grosa' and 'flaco' → 'flaca'. _(Gendered forms are missing; learners will call women 'un capo'.)_
- **low** `missing` chapa — "Tener chapa" means having status or reputation. Also sheet metal... → Add: 'Young people also say "está chapa": he's crazy.' _('Estar chapa' (crazy) is very common today and looks like the same word.)_
- **low** `weird` guarango — No seas guarango y saludá a tu tía. → No seas guarango, no hables así en la mesa. (en: 'Don't be crude, don't talk like that at the table.') _('Guarango' is crude/vulgar; not greeting someone is 'maleducado', so the example shows the wrong meaning.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear` ñeri — Street slang for a friend, from "compañero". Also used for a rough, streetwise guy. → Add: 'Slang from poor neighborhoods and cumbia/trap music. Good to understand; sounds strange from a foreigner.' _(Strong class and register marker; the learner should recognize it, not use it.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear` vieja — Affectionate, not rude: "mi vieja" is my mom... → Add: 'Only with "mi/tu". "Una vieja" or "esa vieja" is a rude way to say old woman.' _(Without the possessive the word is insulting.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear?` cumplemés — Young couples celebrate each month together. → Note: 'A month anniversary: used for a baby's first months and by young couples.' _(Most common use is for babies; the note explains a habit and not the word.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` trapito — El trapito me pidió quinientos pesos para cuidar el auto. → El trapito me pidió cinco lucas para cuidar el auto. (en: 'five thousand pesos') _(500 pesos is not a realistic price any more; the sentence looks outdated.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` cero — I have zero desire to cook today, let's order something. → I really don't feel like cooking today, let's order something. _('Zero desire' is stiff English; plain version is clearer.)_
- **low** `en_hard` buchón — Who was the snitch who told mom? / note: tattletale or informer → en example: 'Who told mom? Who was it?' or keep the card wording: 'Who was the one who told on us to mom?' Note: 'someone who tells on others'. _('Snitch' and 'tattletale' are hard for a B1 English reader.)_
- **low** `en_hard` kiosquero — the tiny shop selling candy, smokes and drinks → the tiny shop selling candy, cigarettes and drinks _('Smokes' is English slang.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` tipo — See you around nine at the bar door. → See you around nine at the door of the bar. _('At the bar door' is unnatural English.)_
- **low** `en_wrong` opa — en: whoa · example en: Oops! You almost dropped the glass. → en: 'whoa, oops' _(Main line and example translation use different words for the same card.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear` pedorro — From "pedo", fart, but used casually by everyone. → From "pedo", fart. Casual and a bit crude: fine with friends, not in formal situations. _('Used by everyone' hides that it is mildly crude.)_

### slang2

- **medium** `not_relevant` cesto de basura — es: cesto de basura → Replace the card with "tacho" (en: trash can; note: "tacho de basura"; example: "Tirá el papel en el tacho.") _(The card's own note says people say "tacho". Teach the word people use.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` sorbete — In Spain it's "pajita"; in Argentina you'd say "sorbete" or "pajita". → The drinking straw. Argentines say "sorbete" or "pajita"; both are understood everywhere. _(Note contradicts itself: pajita is given as both the Spain word and the Argentine word.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` napo — en: Neapolitan pizza → en: tomato and garlic pizza. Note: add 'Also short for "milanesa a la napolitana": "una mila napo".' _("Neapolitan pizza" means Naples-style pizza in English. Napo is also very often the milanesa.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` bife de chorizo — Pedí un bife de chorizo jugoso con ensalada. / I ordered a juicy steak with salad. → I ordered a sirloin steak, medium rare, with salad. Add to note: 'Doneness: "jugoso" (rare/medium rare), "a punto" (medium), "cocido" (well done).' _(On a menu order "jugoso" is how cooked the meat is, not "juicy". Useful to teach.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` entraña — Para mí, una entraña jugosa con papas fritas. / For me, a juicy skirt steak with fries. → For me, a skirt steak, medium rare, with fries. _(Same as above: "jugosa" in an order means rare/medium rare.)_

### slang3

- **high** `not_argentine` juguera — en: blender / Pasame la juguera que hago un licuado. → Replace the card with `licuadora` = blender (example: "Pasame la licuadora que hago un licuado."). - **medium** `es_wrong` calentarse — No te calentés, fue sin querer. (gap: calentés) → "No te calientes, fue sin querer." gap: calientes _(Standard porteño negative is no te calientes; the card's own note says so too.)_

- **medium** `en_wrong` partido — note: Also means match or party. → "Also means a match (game) or a political party." _(Partido never means a party with friends (fiesta). Learner would misuse it.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` living — en: lounge, main room → en: "living room" _(Main line should match the example and plain English; lounge is British and unclear.)_
- **medium** `not_argentine` villa miseria — es: villa miseria / Creció en una villa miseria y hoy es médico. → Make the card `villa`: "Creció en una villa y hoy es médico." - **medium** `missing` guarda — note: The ticket inspector on trains and, in the past, on buses. → Add: "¡Guarda!" = watch out, careful ("Guarda con el escalón"). Consider making that the main card, level 1. _(The interjection is far more common and useful than the train job.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` mucama — note: A maid in a house or hotel. → Note: "Normal for hotel staff. For someone who cleans a home it sounds old and classist; say 'la empleada' or 'la señora que limpia'." _(Learner could offend by calling a home worker mucama.)_

- **medium** `not_relevant` ñata — level 2 / Casual for nose. → Level 3 + tag "Old-fashioned"; say it survives mostly in the tango line and in "ñato" (snub-nosed, also a nickname). _(Almost nobody says ñata for nose today; people say nariz or naso.)_

- **medium** `not_relevant` pollera tubo — es: pollera tubo / en: pencil skirt → Make the card `pollera` = skirt ("Me puse una pollera para la entrevista"); mention pollera tubo in the note. _(Pollera is the key Argentine word; the pencil-skirt compound is niche.)_

- **low** `not_relevant` sortija — level 2 → Level 3, or drop. _(Real word, but only useful at a kids' merry-go-round. Niche.)_

- **low** `not_relevant?` diariero — The person who sells papers at a kiosk → Note: "at a 'puesto de diarios'. Also 'canillita'. Fewer every year." _(Real word but fading with print papers; kiosk suggests the candy kiosco.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` bañadera — Also an old open-top bus rented for groups. → Remove that sentence. _(Obsolete meaning; filler that confuses.)_
- **low** `level?` detonado — level 1 → Level 2. _(Younger slang, less basic than the other level-1 mood words.)_
- **low** `tip_unclear?` pieza — Everyday word for a bedroom → Add: "'Cuarto' and 'habitación' are just as common." _(Pieza is not the only everyday word; many porteños say cuarto.)_

## Culture


### culture-a

- **high** `missing` sos-invitado / 'The host usually buys the meat' — The host usually buys the meat, or friends split the cost. Guests bring **vino**, drinks, dessert or **hielo**. → Add the phrases: **¿Qué llevo?** (What should I bring?) and **¿Cuánto es por cabeza?** / **Después dividimos** (how much each / we split it later). _(The single most useful thing to say when invited is missing; splitting the bill among friends is standard.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong` que-es-el-mate / 'By law, mate is Argentina's infusión nacional' — By law, mate is Argentina's **infusión nacional**: the national drink. → By law (since 2013), mate is Argentina's **infusión nacional**, the national infusion. (Wine got the title of national drink the same day.) _(Ley 26.871 says 'infusión nacional'; Ley 26.870 makes wine the 'bebida nacional'. 'National drink' is wine.)_

Don't share: say **estoy resfriado, paso**. Since the pandemic, many people bring their own mate, and nobody minds." _(Sharing habits changed after 2020; a newcomer should know own-mate is normal and not rude.)_
- **medium** `repetitive` mate.yaml + asado.yaml / repeated joke — "they'll happily tell you why yours is wrong" · "they'll defend it to the death" · "each one is sure its way is the right way" · "Ask two Argentines which is best: three opinions" · "each swear theirs is the best" · "same arguments" → Keep two at most (yerba brand, leña vs carbón). Rewrite the others as plain facts. _(The 'Argentines argue about everything' joke appears six-plus times; it becomes a stereotype.)_
- **medium** `en_hard` mate.yaml + asado.yaml / English idiom — "growers cracked it again" · "The cebador takes the hit" · "so nobody gives you the look" · "What's the jab?" / "a political dig" · "the brave stuff" · "crisps up" · "Company earns you snacks" → "growers learned how again" · "The cebador drinks it so nobody else has to" · "so nobody looks at you funny" → "so you don't get it wrong" · "What's the insult?" / "a political insult" · "the parts for brave eaters" · "gets crispy" · "Stay close and you get to taste first" _(House style is plain English for B1 readers; these idioms need a native ear.)_
- **medium** `missing` el-fuego / 'The parrilla is the grill' — The **parrilla** is the grill: an iron grate, often built into the backyard in brick. → Add: "A **parrilla** is also a steakhouse: **Vamos a una parrilla** = let's go eat grilled meat." _(Most newcomers first eat asado at a restaurant parrilla; the second meaning is never taught.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` el-fuego / 'How do you like it?' — Many say **a punto**, medium. Others want **jugoso**, pink, or **bien cocido**, well done. - **low** `weird` horarios-y-mesa / card 'That's why the sobremesa exists' — That's why the **sobremesa** exists: the long chat after the meal → 'The reason is the **sobremesa**: the long chat after the meal ...' _(Cause is backwards: the bill waits because of the sobremesa, not the other way round.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` horarios-y-mesa / Pro tip vaquita — Everyone throwing money into one pot is **hacer una vaquita**. Nobody counts who ate the extra slice. → 'Splitting the bill evenly: **“¿Dividimos?”** Pooling money to buy something together (the asado, a gift) is **hacer una vaquita**.' _(Vaquita is pooling money to buy something, not really splitting a restaurant bill; give the phrase people use.)_
- **low** `missing` horarios-y-mesa / card 'Argentines eat late' — Lunch around one, dinner around **ten**. → Add one line on breakfast: 'Breakfast is small and sweet: **café con leche** and two **medialunas** or toast.' _(Newcomers expect a big breakfast; the meal map skips it.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` horarios-y-mesa / card 'Kids keep the same hours' — Near midnight, restaurants are full of families → 'At eleven at night, you still see families in restaurants ...' _(Exaggerated; true on weekends and holidays, not a general rule.)_
- **low** `experience?` empanadas / choice salteña vs tucumana — Only the salteña has potato / Only the tucumana is fried / Only the salteña has egg → Keep answer. Prompt: 'One famous difference between a salteña and a tucumana?' _(Answer is right, but nobody can guess it; 'the big difference' oversells one of several.)_
- **low** `experience?` empanadas / Pro tip — Bite a corner first and lean over the plate. → Add the local saying: 'A juicy empanada is eaten **con las piernas abiertas**, legs apart, so the juice misses your pants.' _(The well-known northern saying is more memorable and real than the generic advice.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` pizza-portena / card fugazzeta — Then there's the **fugazzeta**: a mountain of onion over cheese. Order it **rellena** and the cheese comes stuffed inside the dough too. → Add: '**Fugazza** is onion only, no cheese.' _(Fugazza vs fugazzeta is a classic ordering mistake; one clause prevents it.)_
- **low** `experience?` pizza-portena / class length — 6 pages, ends on a question → Add a closing card (e.g. name Güerrin / El Cuartito, or 'pizza is eaten with knife and fork at the table, by hand at the counter'). _(Shortest class; other classes end with a tip card, this one stops abruptly.)_
- **low** `experience` herencia-italiana / title + card nona — title 'Nonna's kitchen'; 'Grandma and grandpa are even **nona** and **nono**.' → Title 'La cocina de la nona'; card: 'In many families, grandma and grandpa are **la nona** and **el nono**.' _(Italian spelling in title vs Argentine in card; most people still say abuela/abuelo.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` herencia-italiana / card milanesa — thin beef, breaded and fried ... what's waiting in every lunchbox the day after → 'thin beef or chicken, breaded and fried or baked. The leftovers become tomorrow's **sánguche de milanesa**.' Add: 'Everyone says **mila**. Classic sides: **papas fritas** or **puré**.' _(Chicken milanesa is as common; 'lunchbox' is not the local picture, the sandwich is. 'Mila' is must-know.)_
- **low** `experience` herencia-italiana / choice 'Why the 29th?' — By then the salary was gone, and gnocchi are cheap ... There's also an Italian legend of a saint → Prompt: 'Why the 29th? The practical explanation:' and name the saint: 'San Pantaleón'. _(Two explanations exist, so the question should say which one it wants.)_
- **low** `weird` herencia-italiana / card ñoqui jab — Which is why **ñoqui** is also a jab at someone accused of holding a public job and only showing up around the 29th. To get paid. → 'So a **ñoqui** is also someone with a public job who never works and only shows up at the end of the month, to get paid. It is an insult.' _(Sentence is long and tangled; 'jab' is an idiom; learner should know it is insulting.)_
- **low** `missing` guisos-y-helado / card guiso — a **guiso**, a hearty home stew. One pot, cheap cuts, whatever's in the fridge → Name the everyday one: 'The classic is **guiso de lentejas**, lentil stew.' _(Lentil stew is the guiso every Argentine means; the class jumps straight to festive locro.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` guisos-y-helado / card 'Locro is no immigrant dish' — On top goes **quiquirimichi**, a spicy red fat. → 'On the side comes a spicy red sauce of oil, paprika and green onion. Ask: **“¿Tiene picante?”**' _(It is a sauce of oil/fat with paprika and green onion, added to taste; most porteños do not know the word.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` guisos-y-helado / choice locro — On **25 de mayo** and **9 de julio**, locro is the patriotic dish. → Add what the dates are: '25 de mayo (the 1810 revolution) and 9 de julio (independence, 1816)', and 'also on May 1st'. _(Explain repeats the answer without explaining; dates mean nothing to a newcomer.)_
- **low** `experience` guisos-y-helado / slug + title — slug 'guisos-y-helado', title 'Stews and corn' → Rename slug to 'guisos-y-maiz' if nothing depends on it. _(Slug says ice cream, class has none (helado is its own class).)_
- **low** `en_wrong` helado / choice kilo delivered — Helado comes to your door in a foam box: **un cuarto**, **medio** or **un kilo**. → Helado comes to your door in a foam tub: **un cuarto** (250 g), **medio kilo** or **un kilo**. _(It is a tub, not a box; 'medio' alone is unclear and 'cuarto' is never explained as 250 g.)_
- **low** `experience?` helado / card 'Italian immigrants brought their helado' — There's a **heladería** on every other corner, and people eat it even in winter. → 'There are heladerías in every neighborhood, open late, and people eat helado even in winter.' _('Every other corner' is brochure exaggeration; open-late is the more useful fact.)_
- **low** `missing?` section / topics — Six classes: hours, empanadas, pizza, Italian, stews, helado → Consider one page on the **picada** and **vermut** (shared board before dinner) and one on being vegetarian ('**¿Tenés algo sin carne?**'). _(Common social food moment and a common newcomer need, not covered here.)_

### culture-c

- **high** `missing` moverse / whole class — No card says how you pay on the bondi or subte → Add a card: "You can't pay cash on the bondi. Tap a **SUBE** card (sold at kioscos and subte stations) or a contactless bank card or phone. Tell the driver where you're going: **“Hasta Plaza Italia.”**" _(First thing a newcomer needs. Buenos Aires Herald: buses took contactless cards from Dec 2024; SUBE still standard.)_
- **high** `missing?` patagonia / Ushuaia + el-interior / Antarctica question — Tierra del Fuego province and the official map are explained with Antarctica only → Add a card: the same province includes the **Islas Malvinas**. In Argentina always say Malvinas, never "Falklands"; signs say **“Las Malvinas son argentinas”**. _(The one piece of etiquette a foreigner must know; skip only if the history section already says it.)_
- **medium** `missing` moverse / "The bondi only stops if you ask" — The bondi only stops if you ask. When your line comes, stick your arm out, or it drives right past you. → Add the other half: "To get off, press the button (**el timbre**) before your stop and leave by the back door." _("Only stops if you ask" is true for getting off too; the card teaches only getting on.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong` vida-portena / "El Ateneo Grand Splendid" — Card on Avenida Corrientes, then directly: "**El Ateneo Grand Splendid** ... used to be something else. What?" → Say where it is: "On Avenida **Santa Fe**, El Ateneo Grand Splendid…" or move the question away from the Corrientes card. _(The Ateneo is on Av. Santa Fe 1860, not Corrientes; the order makes learners think it is on Corrientes.)_
- **medium** `missing?` section summary + vida-portena — summary: "...the city that never goes to bed" but no card about the hours → Add a card: dinner at 9:30–10 pm, restaurants empty at 8, bars fill after midnight, **boliches** open around 2 am. _(The summary promises it and the timetable shocks every newcomer; skip only if Costumbres already covers it.)_
- **medium** `missing` barrios or moverse — Nothing on how porteños give addresses and directions → Add a card: addresses are given as two streets, **“Corrientes y Callao”**, and distance in blocks: **“Son cinco cuadras.”** _(You need this in every taxi and every time you ask the way; very porteño and easy to teach.)_
- **medium** `missing` iconos-de-la-ciudad / "At a classic café like the Tortoni" — The waiter won't bring the check until you ask. → Add the phrase: "…until you ask: **“¿Me cobrás?”** or **“La cuenta, por favor.”**" _(The card says you must ask but does not teach what to say.)_
- **medium** `missing` iconos-de-la-ciudad / whole class — Casa Rosada card, but no Plaza de Mayo → Add a card on **Plaza de Mayo**: in front of the Casa Rosada, where the country celebrates and protests, and where the **Madres de Plaza de Mayo** have marched every Thursday since 1977. _(It is the most important public place in Argentina and is missing from the city icons class.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong` noroeste / "take a shot of something on an empty stomach" — Question sits in the Noroeste class right after Pachamama; explain: "**Caña con ruda**: cane liquor steeped with rue... keeps the bad luck of winter away" → Add to explain: "The custom is Guaraní, from the northeast, not Andean, but it shares the date." Or move the question to the Litoral class. _(Sources (Cadena 3, El Litoral) say it is a Guaraní tradition from the Litoral; here it reads as an Andean one.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong` cuyo / "Behind the city stands the Aconcagua" — Behind the city stands the **Aconcagua**: almost 7,000 meters... On the road to Chile you can see its snowy face. → "About three hours west of the city, on the road to Chile, stands **Aconcagua**: almost 7,000 meters, the highest mountain outside Asia. You don't need to climb it: there's a viewpoint by the road." _(Aconcagua is about 180 km by road from Mendoza city and cannot be seen from it. English drops "the".)_
- **medium** `missing` litoral / whole class — No food or drink of the Litoral → Add a card: **tereré** (mate with ice-cold water or juice) and **chipá** (warm cheese bread sold on every corner and bus). _(These are what a visitor is actually offered there; more useful than the Eleanor Roosevelt quote.)_
- **medium** `missing` patagonia / whole class — Only Welsh settlers, Alps-like Bariloche, tourists → Add a card: Patagonia is the land of the **Mapuche** and **Tehuelche**; many place names are theirs (Nahuel Huapi, Neuquén, Chubut). _(Noroeste and Litoral name their native peoples; Patagonia reads as if it was empty before Europeans.)_
- **medium** `missing?` whole section — Classes: overview, Noroeste, Cuyo, Córdoba, Litoral, Patagonia → Add a class on the pampa and the Atlantic coast: **el campo**, estancias, gauchos, and **Mar del Plata**; **“Me voy a la costa”** is what half of Buenos Aires does in January. _(The region most Argentines live in or holiday in is missing; "la costa" comes up in every summer chat.)_
- **medium** `missing` noroeste / whole class — 7 pages: landscape, coca (2 pages), Pachamama, caña con ruda, carnival → Replace the second coca card or add one on **empanadas** (salteñas vs tucumanas, each province swears theirs are best) and the **peña**, the place to eat and hear **folklore**. _(Food and folklore are what visitors meet first; Tucumán is never named. Coca takes a third of the class.)_
- **low** `experience` vida-portena / title — Five things you'll notice in your first week → "Things you'll notice in your first week" (or cut to exactly five) _(The class has seven ideas, not five; and a bookshop quiz is not something you "notice".)_
- **low** `experience` iconos-de-la-ciudad / "At a classic café like the Tortoni" — At a classic café like the **Tortoni**, order a **cortado** and stay two hours. → "At any neighborhood café, order a **cortado** (espresso with a little milk) and stay two hours." Mention the Tortoni only as the famous one, with a line at the door. _(The Tortoni is the tourist café with a queue outside; the no-rush habit is true of ordinary cafés. Cortado is not explained.)_
- **low** `en_hard` barrios / "La Boca sits where the Riachuelo" — built houses of wood and **chapa**, painted, the story goes, with leftover paint → "built houses of wood and **chapa** (metal sheets), painted, the story goes, with paint left over from the shipyards" _(Chapa is bolded but never explained; also "the river" is never named (Río de la Plata).)_
- **low** `missing` barrios / "La Boca" card — La Boca card and Caminito question → Add one line: Caminito is two tourist blocks; locals tell you not to wander far from it, especially at night. And mention Boca Juniors' stadium, **la Bombonera**. _(Standard local advice for visitors, and the Bombonera is what most people come to La Boca for.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` barrios / "Palermo is the biggest barrio" — people keep inventing sub-barrios: **Palermo Soho**, **Palermo Hollywood**, Palermo Chico → Replace Palermo Chico with an invented one, e.g. "Palermo Queens" (the joke name for Villa Crespo). _(Palermo Chico is an old, traditional name from the 1910s, not a recent real-estate invention.)_
- **low** `not_relevant` moverse / "Taxis are black and yellow" — Taxis are black and yellow, and porteños call them **tachos**. → Make it useful: "A free taxi shows a red **LIBRE** light. Porteños call the taxi a **tacho** and the driver a **tachero**." _(Thin card; tachero is heard more than tacho, and how to spot a free taxi is the useful part.)_
- **low** `missing` portenos / "Cross the General Paz avenue" — People out there aren't porteños, and they call the city just **Capital**. → Add: "People from the Province are **bonaerenses**. (To the rest of the country, though, everyone from the metro area is a porteño.)" _(Gives the missing word and the real nuance; people from the provinces do call conurbano people porteños.)_
- **low** `en_hard` portenos / "God is everywhere" question — The provinces have a famous comeback / **agrandados**, full of themselves → "The provinces have a famous saying about this" / "**agrandados**: people who think they are better than everyone" _("Comeback" and "full of themselves" are idioms a B1 reader may not know.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` vida-portena / "The word you'll hear most" — The word you'll hear most in your first week: **¡Ojo!** → "A word you'll hear a lot in your first week: **¡Ojo!**" _(Exaggerated; che, dale or bueno are heard far more.)_
- **low** `experience` portenos + regiones.yaml el-interior — Both classes teach: porteños vs provinces, capital thinks it is the country, provincial pride, "el interior" → Keep the rivalry in `portenos`; in `el-interior` cut the Salta card or the "no wonder the capital thinks it is the country" line. _(Same idea told twice in two sections; also the regiones slug is "el-interior", the word BA class says to avoid.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` noroeste / caña con ruda explain — One shot on 1 August keeps the bad luck of winter away → "Three sips (some say seven) on 1 August keep away the illnesses and bad luck of August" _(Tradition is three to seven sips, against the ills of August; also "steeped" is hard English (use "soaked").)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` cuyo / siesta card + title — title "Cuyo: wine, water and the siesta" / "Here it's the schedule: shops shut after lunch" → Add "as in most of the provinces" and the etiquette: "Don't call or ring a doorbell between 2 and 5." _(The siesta is the rule across the north and center too, not a Cuyo thing; the etiquette is the useful part.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` litoral / "Rosario, Argentina's third city" — order a **liso**, a draft beer in a straight glass → "order a **liso**, the province's small smooth glass of draft beer" _(La Nación/La Capital: the liso is a Santa Fe tradition (born in Santa Fe city), about 255 cm³; fine for Rosario but describe it right.)_
- **low** `missing` litoral / Rosario card — Rosarinos will remind you that Messi was born here. → Add: "…and that the Argentine flag was raised for the first time here, in 1812." _(The Monumento a la Bandera is Rosario's main symbol and a basic fact every Argentine knows.)_
- **low** `experience` litoral / whole class — 10 pages, 3 questions; two cards on Iguazú plus the Roosevelt quote → Merge the Garganta del Diablo card into the Iguazú explain and drop the Roosevelt line. _(Longest class of the section; the quote is the usual brochure line and unverified.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong` patagonia / Tren del Fin del Mundo explain — Ushuaia began as a prison town. → "Ushuaia grew up around a prison." _(The town was founded in 1884 as a naval post; the prison came in 1902 and made it grow.)_
- **low** `experience` patagonia / "Perito Moreno" card — Card: "For years it kept building an ice bridge" then question, then explain "doubt it will build that ice bridge again" → In the card say what the bridge is: "Every few years the ice reached the shore, dammed the lake and then broke in a huge collapse, shown live on TV." _("Ice bridge across the lake" is unclear, and "each collapse was broadcast live" is a little exaggerated.)_
- **low** `experience?` noroeste / "Fly two hours north" — **Salta** and **Jujuy** feel closer to Bolivia than to Palermo → "**Salta** and **Jujuy** are Andean Argentina: adobe villages, llamas, ponchos…" _(People from Salta and Jujuy can find "more Bolivia than Argentina" comparisons offensive.)_
- **low** `en_hard` noroeste / "Every 1 de agosto" — Every **1 de agosto** ... food, coca, corn beer and wine → "Every **primero de agosto** (1 August) ... food, coca, **chicha** (corn beer) and wine" _(The date is said "primero de agosto"; chicha is the word the learner will hear.)_
- **low** `en_hard` noroeste / coca question + explain — has a bulging cheek / keep a wad of coca leaves in their cheek / It's no scandal → "has one cheek full of something" / "keep a ball of coca leaves in their cheek" / "Nobody is shocked" _("Bulging" and "wad" are hard words for B1 readers.)_
- **low** `en_hard` cordoba / Villa General Belgrano explain — the warship **Graf Spee** was scuttled off Montevideo. Its crew was interned in Argentina → "the German warship **Graf Spee** was sunk by its own crew near Montevideo. The sailors were held in Argentina until the war ended" _("Scuttled" and "interned" are rare words. Also say the town was already founded by Germans.)_
- **low** `experience` cordoba / summary — The province that talks slower, parties harder and jokes about everything → "The province that sings when it talks, parties hard and jokes about everything" _(The tonada is a melody, not slow speech; "slower" repeats the porteño stereotype of the provinces.)_
- **low** `experience` cordoba / "Cordobeses are famous for their humor" — Cordobeses are famous for their humor. Their signature word is **culiao**. → Split: one card on humor (fast jokes, nicknames for everyone), one on **culiao**. Add **La Mona Jiménez** to the cuarteto card. _(Two unrelated ideas on one card; the humor claim gets no example. La Mona is the name every Argentine links to cuarteto.)_
- **low** `en_hard` cuyo / acequia + cordoba / fernet cards — Falling into an acequia is a rite of passage / Pace yourself. → "Everyone falls into an acequia once" / "Drink slowly." _(Idioms; house style is plain English.)_
- **low** `experience` el-interior / "Provincial pride runs deep" — Tell a girl from Salta who moved to Buenos Aires that she's porteña now → "Tell someone from Salta who has lived in Buenos Aires for ten years that they're porteño now" _("A girl" for an adult woman reads badly; "ten years" makes the point stronger.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` el-interior / "Getting around means the micro" — Getting around means the **micro**, the long-distance bus. Twenty hours overnight ... is completely normal. → "The classic way to get around is the **micro**… Twenty hours in a **coche cama** is normal, though cheap flights now take many of those trips." _(A bit dated: low-cost flights replaced much long-distance bus travel. Note that in Mendoza "micro" is the city bus.)_

### culture-d

- **medium** `es_wrong?` el-beso / "Arrive at a party of twelve" — you **saludás a todos**: you go around and kiss → you **saludás a todos uno por uno**: you go around and kiss (or teach the noun phrase: "**saludar uno por uno**") _("Saludás a todos" alone does not carry the idea taught; a group "hola" is also saludar a todos.)_
- **medium** `tip_unclear` el-beso / "Then comes ¿Todo bien?" — **¿Qué hacés?** Not real questions, just hello. → Add: "**¿Qué hacés?** looks like 'what are you doing?' but here it only means 'hi'. Answer **“Todo bien, ¿y vos?”**, not what you are doing." _(No translation given; learners will answer literally. This is a classic newcomer mistake.)_
- **medium** `missing` el-beso (whole class) — Class covers only the hello kiss → Add one card: you kiss everyone again when you leave, and which cheek (lean to your left, right cheeks touch). Add **chau** as the goodbye word. _(Newcomers hesitate on which side and do not know the goodbye round; goodbye kiss only hinted in another class.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong?` salir-de-noche / choice "Previa at Tomi's" — At nine the night hasn't started. The previa gets going around midnight. → At nine people are just starting dinner. The previa gets going around eleven or midnight. _(Previas usually start 22:30-23:30 so people reach the boliche by 2; "midnight" alone is late.)_
- **medium** `missing` salir-de-noche (whole class) — Class is only previa + boliche + after → Add one card on the more common plan: dinner at 9:30-10 pm, then **un bar** or **una birra** with friends; and that restaurants are empty at 7 pm. _(Most adult learners will go to dinner and bars, not boliches; late dinner hour is the key fact.)_
- **medium** `experience` sin-filtro / "Your aunt sees you after the holidays" — She means it warmly, like “you look well fed.” → "She doesn't mean it as an insult. For her generation it is just an observation, like 'you got a haircut'." _(Presents weight comments as warm; many Argentines today find them unwelcome. Softer framing avoids endorsing it.)_
- **medium** `missing` sin-filtro (whole class) — "No filter" covers body comments and prices only → Add a card: people ask direct personal questions early (¿Tenés novio? ¿De dónde sos? ¿Qué hacés acá?), interrupt and talk over each other, and give opinions on politics and football; it is interest, not rudeness. _(Directness in conversation is the main culture shock; more useful than the second gauchada card.)_
- **medium** `missing?` el-calendario (whole class) — Friends' Day, spring, long weekends, birthdays → Add one card on the big national dates a newcomer will meet: **25 de Mayo** and **9 de Julio** (with locro and escarapela), and **24 de marzo** as a solemn memorial day, not a party. _(Calendar class skips the patriotic and memorial holidays; 24 March needs sensitivity. Skip if covered in historia files.)_
- **medium** `missing?` section summary / overall — Six classes: kiss, time, going out, no filter, Christmas, calendar → Add a short etiquette class: **permiso** when entering a home or passing, **buen provecho**, **gracias** means "no more" in a mate round, greeting the shopkeeper with **buenas**, **disculpá** vs **perdón**, no shoes-off rule, keep your phone out of sight on the street. _(Everyday what-to-say/what-not-to-do etiquette is the most practical part of "customs" and is absent here.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` expresiones-del-dia / choice explain "Mandar fruta" — **Mandar fruta** is winging it with words. → **Mandar fruta** is talking nonsense or making things up as if you knew. _("Winging it" is idiom and means improvising, not saying nonsense; meaning is off and hard.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` expresiones-del-dia / "le hacés la gamba" — You **le hacés la gamba**: you lend her your leg. It means keeping someone company when it counts. → You **le hacés la gamba**: literally "you do the leg for her". It means doing someone a favor or backing them up, often by going along. Ask for it: **“¿Me hacés la gamba?”** _(Literal gloss is wrong (hacer, not prestar) and the meaning is wider than keeping company.)_
- **medium** `missing?` expresiones-del-dia (whole class) — 7 expressions: al horno, cayó la ficha, ponete las pilas, garrón, mandar fruta, hacer la gamba, buena onda → Add or swap in the higher-frequency ones: **ya fue** (forget it), **no da** (not OK), **de una** (sure, let's go), **me estás cargando** (you're kidding), **ni ahí** (no way), **es lo que hay** (it is what it is). _(These are heard far more often than "hacer la gamba"; skip if the Words hub already teaches them.)_
- **medium** `experience` filosofia-criolla / "viveza criolla" — Pull it off and you're a **vivo**. Play fair and you're a **gil**, a sucker. Argentines joke about it, and complain too. → "Pull it off and some call you a **vivo**. Many Argentines hate it and blame it for the country's problems. **No te hagas el vivo** means: don't try to be clever with me." _(Reads as "Argentines cheat and honest people are suckers"; stereotype. Reframe as a criticized habit and add the useful phrase.)_
- **medium** `missing` filosofia-criolla (whole class) — No "es lo que hay" / "no pasa nada" / "ya fue" → Add a card for **es lo que hay** (it is what it is), the resigned shrug used every day, far more than "Dios es argentino". _(The most-used "philosophy" phrase in daily speech is missing.)_
- **low** `not_argentine` el-beso / "Then comes ¿Todo bien?" — **“Todo bien, ¿vos?”** is the whole answer. → **“Todo bien, ¿y vos?”** is the whole answer. _(The natural reply is "¿y vos?"; without "y" it sounds clipped.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` el-beso / "Arrive at a party of twelve" — you go around and kiss every single person, strangers included → Add a limit: "In a small or medium group. At a big party, a loud **“¡Hola, buenas!”** to the room and kisses for the people near you." _(True for home gatherings; overstated as a rule for any party size.)_
- **low** `en_hard` la-hora-argentina / "Invited to dinner at someone's home" — Arriving early is the real faux pas. → Arriving early is the real mistake: the host is still in the shower. _("Faux pas" is not plain English for a B1 reader.)_
- **low** `fact_wrong?` la-hora-argentina / "That's social life only" — Work, classes and the doctor run on the clock. → "For work, classes and the doctor, be on time, or at least text. (The doctor may still keep you waiting.)" _(Doctors' appointments in Argentina commonly run late; the patient must be punctual, the clock is not.)_
- **low** `en_hard` la-hora-argentina / choice "ya salgo" — **Ya salgo** has padding built in → **Ya salgo** always includes some extra time _("Padding built in" is idiomatic; hard for non-native readers.)_
- **low** `missing` la-hora-argentina / "Never show up empty-handed" — The host will say **“no traigas nada”** ... Bring wine or dessert anyway. → Add the phrase the guest says first: **“¿Qué llevo?”** (What should I bring?). Mention **helado** as the classic dessert to bring. _(Teaches what the host says but not the guest's line, which the learner actually needs.)_
- **low** `weird` la-hora-argentina / choice "bueno, me voy yendo" — options: About half an hour / About two minutes / About ten minutes → Keep answer; make explain say it: "Half an hour, easily. ### culture-f

- **high** `missing` la-puta-madre / class — (no pedo / cagar / joder families) → Add a class or 2-3 cards: **al pedo** (pointless), **en pedo** (drunk), **ni en pedo** (no way), **de pedo** (by luck); **cagarse de risa**, **una cagada**, **me cagó**; **no jodas / me estás jodiendo**; **carajo**. _(These are the most frequent vulgar expressions in daily talk, far more than la concha de tu madre, and are absent.)_
- **high** `missing` section — (no card on hijo de puta / as praise) → Add: **hijo de puta** is a heavy insult, but '¡qué hijo de puta!' after a great goal or joke is admiration. Understand, do not say. _(Extremely common and confusing for foreigners; fits the section's 'context decides' theme exactly.)_
- **high** `missing` section — (slurs only mentioned for stadium chants) → Add a card of words never to repeat: **puto/trolo** (anti-gay), **mogólico** (ableist), **negro de mierda** (classist/racist), **bolita/paragua** (xenophobic). And note that **negro/gordo/flaco** as nicknames are affectionate, not insults. _(A newcomer hears these daily and cannot tell slur from nickname; biggest register gap in the section.)_
- **medium** `en_wrong` lunfardo / choice 'The city bus is the bondi' — Where does the word come from, the story goes? → According to the usual story, where does the word come from? _(Broken English word order; hard to parse.)_
- **medium** `missing` lunfardo / class — (only laburo, bondi, chamuyo, mina shown) → Add one card with everyday survivors: guita (money), pibe/piba (kid), morfar (to eat), birra (beer), fiaca (laziness). _(A class called Lunfardo teaches only four words; guita and pibe are heard far more than chamuyo.)_
- **medium** `missing` manos-y-chat / card 'Two more you'll see daily' — Flat hand rocking… más o menos. Finger pulling down your lower eyelid… ¡ojo! → Add the chin flick: back of the fingers brushed forward from under the chin = 'ni idea' / 'I don't know'. _(The most distinctively Argentine gesture is missing; in Italy it means 'I don't care', so foreigners misread it.)_
- **medium** `fact_wrong` manos-y-chat / card 'When they do type' — **tqm**, te quiero mucho, closes half the chats in the country. → Show the common ones: **q** (que), **xq** (porque), **tmb** (también), **dsp** (después), **ntp** (no te preocupes), **jajaja**. tqm closes many family chats. _(Exaggerated; tqm is mostly teens and moms. Everyday shortcuts are more useful to read.)_
- **medium** `missing` section — (no card on dale) → Add **dale** somewhere: ok / come on / go ahead; the word a newcomer hears most after che. _(A section on how Argentines talk covers che, re, posta, viste, but not dale.)_

- **low** `missing?` malvinas / whole class — Nothing on the people living on the islands or on Britain's position → One neutral line: 'About 3,500 people live there and want to stay British; Argentina says the question is about territory, to be settled by talks. Also explain adds nothing but the count; say why (each one resigned or was only a caretaker). _(Explain repeats the answer without explaining; 'came and went' is false for the fifth, who governed 16 months.)_
- **low** `missing` democracia-y-crisis / 'Then the one-to-one peso ended' — the devaluation wiped out much of people's savings → Add: 'Dollar deposits were turned into pesos by force, and more than half the country fell below the poverty line.' _(Forced 'pesificación' and 50%+ poverty are why 2001 still shapes behaviour.)_

- **low** `fact_wrong` pensar-en-dolares / 'For years buying dollars was capped' — even a **dólar Coldplay** for concert tickets → even a **dólar Coldplay** for bringing foreign bands to play _(It was the rate promoters paid for foreign artists, not a rate for buying tickets.)_

### culture-overview

- **high** `missing` moverse — Class covers bondi history, arm out, la cola, tachos, subte age. No SUBE anywhere in the tab. → Add a practical class 'SUBE and getting around': you cannot pay cash on bus/subte, buy and load a SUBE at a kiosco, tell the driver your destination, 'pasar la SUBE' for a stranger, ride apps (Cabify/Uber/DiDi), trains, BA Cómo Llego. _(The first thing a newcomer needs to ride anything; the class teaches trivia instead.)_
